4702.t: From Lydian [script needed] (*luwdja, “Luwia”), where the Lydians came to live after being driven away by the Phrygians. Here the -d- is result of affrication of proto-Luwian *-j-.

4766.t: From *δημότ-ιος (-ios) with assibilation of *τ > σ, from δημότης (dēmótēs, “one of the people; fellow citizen”) + -ιος (-ios).

4711.t: From σάμος (sắmos, “seaside hill; dune; height”), from Phoenician 𐤔𐤌𐤀 (sama, “high”).

4712.t: Possibly from τίτο (títo, “sun, day”), which is an Anatolian loan-word, or from τιταίνω (titaínō, “to stretch, to extend”), from τείνω (teínō), or from τίσις (tísis, “retribution”), from τίνω (tínō, “to pay a price as a penalty, expiate”), respectively, as…

4775.t: From διαφαίνω (dĭăphaínō, “to shine; to be manifest”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix).

4719.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewg- (“to lighten up”), which is likely a semantic extension of *h₂ewg- in the usual "to increase" sense.

4714.t: Contracted from *ἀεικεία (*aeikeíā), from ἀ- (ă-, “not”) + εἰκός (eikós, “reasonable, fair”) + -εία (-eíā, abstract noun suffix).

4756.t: From Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to curve, to bend”), the same source as Old Armenian կոր (kor), Lithuanian gur̃nas (“ankle, hip, bone”), and Norwegian kaure (“curly lock of hair”). See also γυῖον (guîon, “hand; limbs”).

4724.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- Proto-Indo-European *-r Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewsér Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwsr̥h₂ Proto-Hellenic *auhrā Ancient Greek αὔρα From Proto-Hellenic *auhrā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwsr̥h₂…

4758.t: From δανείζω (dăneízō, “to lend money”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).

4754.t: Perhaps originally "privilege of age", from Proto-Indo-European *ǵerh₂- (“to grow old”). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀐𐀨 (ke-ra).

4765.t: Unknown, with Beekes suspecting Pre-Greek origin.

4789.t: From δάκνω (dáknō, “to bite”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

4741.t: A connection with γύαλον (gúalon), γωλεός (gōleós), Old Norse kjóll (“ship”) has been considered.

4745.t: From unattested *γέραρ, parallel form of γέρας n (géras, “gift, reward”). Morphologically, stem γερ- + -αρός (-arós).

4743.t: From Latin gaesum, itself from Gaulish *gaisos, from Proto-Celtic *gaisos (“spear”). Compare also χαῖος (khaîos, “shepherd's staff”), Sanskrit हेषस् (héṣas, “missile”).

4784.t: From δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”) + -α (-ā, “nominal suffix”).
